planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all danger of frost in full sun with well-drained soil; growth is fastest in the heat of summer. In central and south Florida this species can self-seed and naturalize readily, so gardeners in those areas should site it where volunteer seedlings can be managed or choose a less seed-prolific alternative.

directions: Bellyache Bush is a fast-growing tropical American shrub grown almost entirely for its striking foliage: new growth emerges deep burgundy and sticky-hairy, maturing to green mottled with wine-red veining and lobed like a small maple leaf. Small red flowers appear in loose clusters nearly year-round in frost-free areas, drawing butterflies, followed by three-lobed seed capsules. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil; established plants tolerate heat and drought and need little supplemental water. CAUTION: all plant parts, especially the seeds and milky sap, are toxic if ingested and can irritate skin — the common name references the severe gastrointestinal poisoning historically caused by the seeds — so site away from children, pets, and livestock, and wear gloves when pruning.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Assessment — Jatropha gossypiifolia
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Jatropha species for Gulf Coast landscapes
ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center — Jatropha species toxicity

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; the tuber offsets over years to form a colony.

directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in early spring in moist, humus-rich soil enriched with leaf mold, in partial to full shade. Arisaema heterophyllum is one of the most distinctive species in the genus, sending up a single leaf divided into an unusually long row of 11 to 19 narrow, arching leaflets that fan out like a feather duster above the green-and-white striped spathe. It is among the more vigorous and cold-hardy Arisaema, tolerating heavier soils and more sun than many relatives, and established clumps slowly build into colonies of many stems. Combine with hostas, ferns, and other woodland perennials in a shaded border; all plant parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are irritating if handled or eaten raw.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; this species wants a bit more warmth and drier winter conditions than the hardiest temperate Arisaema.

directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving winter protection from prolonged wet cold. Arisaema erubescens is a widespread Chinese and Himalayan species with a single umbrella-like leaf held above a purple-brown to green spathe boldly striped in white, the hood drawing out into a long, tapering, upward-curving tip. It is more heat-tolerant than many temperate Arisaema and performs well in warm-summer gardens where it can be grown as a container specimen and moved under cover in regions colder than its hardiness range. As with all Arisaema, the tubers and foliage contain calcium oxalate crystals and are irritating if handled or ingested.

subcategory: hardy Himalayan ginger relative with orchid-like flowers

planting.note: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; mark the site since growth emerges late in spring.

directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, marking the spot since shoots do not appear until late spring. Roscoea beesiana is a Yunnan and Sichuan species named for the Bees Nursery collectors who introduced it, forming compact rosettes of glossy, upright leaves topped by orchid-like flowers in soft primrose-yellow to cream, the lip often marked with fine purple veining. It blooms slightly earlier than R. purpurea and pairs well with hostas and hardy ferns in a woodland or shaded rock garden. Sharp winter drainage is essential, since the fleshy storage roots rot in cold, waterlogged soil.

subcategory: hardy Himalayan ginger relative with orchid-like flowers

planting.note: Plant fleshy root divisions 2-3 inches deep in gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade; this dwarf species suits a shaded rock garden or trough as well as a woodland edge.

directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 2-3 inches deep in gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade, and mark the site since growth emerges late in spring. Roscoea alpina is the smallest widely grown species in the genus, a true alpine from the Himalaya forming diminutive rosettes only a few inches tall, each topped by a single relatively large, purple, orchid-like flower carried close to the foliage. Its compact stature suits shaded rock gardens, troughs, and the front of a woodland border, where it should never be allowed to dry out completely during the growing season. Winter wet is its chief enemy, so a gritty, freely draining soil is essential to keep the fleshy roots from rotting.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring; Sugar Mountain Blue is self-unfruitful and needs a genetically distinct, concurrently blooming pollinizer such as Sugar Mountain Kuma or another early haskap cultivar planted within about 50 feet.

directions: Selected by nurseryman Jim Gilbert of One Green World from Russian Kamchatka-type Lonicera caerulea stock, Sugar Mountain Blue is prized for unusually large, oblong berries with a sweeter, less astringent flavor than many older haskap selections. It ripens very early, often several weeks before most other soft fruit, and needs an unrelated pollinizer variety blooming at the same time to set a full crop. Grow in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil; the upright bush tolerates extreme winter cold but performs poorly in hot, humid summer regions. Renewal-prune out the oldest canes after the first few years to keep yields high.
sources: One Green World Nursery — Haskap/Honeyberry Introductions
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Honeyberry Cultivar Trials

planting.note: Plant in early spring alongside Sugar Mountain Blue or another early-blooming haskap; Kuma was selected specifically as a synchronized-bloom pollen source and bears a lighter, tarter crop of its own edible berries.

directions: Released by One Green World from the same Russian Kamchatka-type breeding line as Sugar Mountain Blue, Kuma was chosen as its dedicated pollinizer partner because its bloom period reliably overlaps with Blue's very early flowering. Kuma also produces a worthwhile crop of its own, smaller and tarter than Sugar Mountain Blue, useful fresh or for preserves. Grow in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; like other haskaps it is extremely cold-hardy but struggles in hot, humid summer climates. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood until the bush is established, then thin older canes periodically to maintain vigor.
sources: One Green World Nursery — Haskap/Honeyberry Introductions
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Honeyberry Cultivar Trials

common_name: Ostsaat Hairy Vetch (German-Bred Winter-Hardy High-Biomass Vetch)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early to mid-fall so plants establish a strong root system before winter; Ostsaat resumes vigorous vining growth in spring and is typically roller-crimped or mowed at early bloom ahead of a no-till cash crop.

directions: Ostsaat is a German-bred hairy vetch selection from Deutsche Saatveredelung, long grown across central Europe and increasingly offered in North American cover-crop mixes for its dependable winter hardiness and heavy biomass output. Like other hairy vetches it fixes substantial nitrogen through its rhizobial root nodules, and its sprawling, vining habit scrambles over a companion cereal such as rye for support while forming a dense weed-suppressing mat. Broadcast or drill inoculated seed into a firm fall seedbed, ideally with a small grain nurse crop to help hold the vines off the ground and ease spring termination. Roll-crimp or mow at early flower to maximize nitrogen contribution and residue longevity ahead of a following warm-season crop.
sources: European cover crop variety trial literature

common_name: Fenn Austrian Winter Pea (Traditional Purple-Flowered Forage Pea)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early to mid-fall so vines establish before hard freezes; Fenn overwinters as a low rosette and resumes vining growth in spring, similar to Melrose and Granger.

directions: Fenn is one of the traditional purple-flowered Austrian winter pea cultivars long used across the southeastern United States as a cool-season legume cover, valued for its winter hardiness and dependable nitrogen fixation. Its indeterminate, sprawling vines climb over a companion cereal such as rye or oats, which both supports the vines and adds carbon-rich residue when the mix is terminated. Newer selections like Melrose and Granger have since surpassed Fenn's yield and disease tolerance in variety trials, but it remains a benchmark cultivar referenced in southern cover-crop research for winter survival. Drill seed into a firm, fertile fall seedbed at adequate depth so the large seeds make good soil contact before cold weather arrives.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Granger Austrian Winter Pea (Upright High-Yielding Forage Pea)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early to mid-fall so plants establish before hard freezes; Granger's more upright growth habit competes well with weeds through winter and eases spring harvest or termination.

directions: Granger is an Austrian winter pea selection bred for a more upright growth habit than older sprawling types like Fenn, giving it better weed competition and easier mechanical harvest while matching their winter survival. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it partners well in a mix with cereal rye or oats, using the grass for support while contributing fixed nitrogen and readily broken-down residue to the following cash crop. Drill inoculated seed into a firm, fertile fall seedbed, since consistent soil moisture at planting is critical for the large seeds to establish before winter dormancy. Its improved yield potential over common Austrian winter pea and Fenn has made it a benchmark cultivar in regional cover-crop variety trials.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension

subcategory: winter annual cover/forage cereal grain hybrid

planting.note: Drill into a prepared fall seedbed in the Southeast several weeks before the first hard freeze so plants tiller well before dormancy; its earlier maturity than standard triticale allows earlier spring termination or grazing.

directions: Trical 342 is an early-maturing forage triticale hybrid widely grown across the southeastern United States for its excellent grazing quality, medium plant height, and good silage value. Beyond forage use it functions as a cover crop, scavenging residual soil nitrogen with its vigorous root system and suppressing weeds with dense fall-to-spring growth, and it carries useful suppression of root-knot nematode populations in rotation. Drill seed into a firm fall seedbed to establish tillering before winter; growth resumes quickly in late winter, reaching grazing or cover height earlier than later-maturing triticale hybrids. Mow, graze, or roll at early heading to terminate as a cover ahead of a summer cash crop.

subcategory: winter annual cover/forage cereal grain hybrid

planting.note: Drill into a prepared fall seedbed several weeks before the first freeze so plants can tiller before dormancy; a regional market-leading forage triticale in the Northeast valued for high dry-matter yield.

directions: TriMark 815 (also sold as Trical 815) is a widely grown forage triticale hybrid and a market-leading variety across the Northeast, prized for high winter and spring dry-matter yield along with good disease resistance. As with other forage triticales, it combines rye's cold hardiness with wheat's palatability, producing a dense, leafy stand usable for grazing, haylage, or as a straight cover crop that scavenges leftover soil nitrogen and improves structure ahead of summer plantings. Drill into a firm fall seedbed early enough to allow full tillering before dormancy; growth resumes vigorously in spring. Cut or roll at early heading for the best balance of forage quality and cover-crop residue when terminating ahead of a following crop.

common_name: Liberty Classic Snapdragon (Compact Early-Flowering Bedding and Cut-Flower Series)

planting.note: Surface-sow the fine seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, since it needs light and should not be covered; transplant out once nights stay above freezing, as young plants tolerate light frost once hardened off.

directions: Liberty Classic is an early-flowering, uniform F1 bedding series bred for compact, well-branched plants that bloom several weeks ahead of taller cut-flower snapdragon types, making it useful for filling the cutting garden while later successions size up. Sold as separate colors including White, Yellow, Bronze, Cherry, Crimson, Rose, and Lavender as well as a blended mix, it produces dense, fully spurred spikes on sturdy 10-15 inch stems that hold up well as short-stemmed cut flowers or mixed bouquet fillers. Its earliness and even habit have made it a long-standing favorite for spring bedding displays as well as market-garden succession cutting. Like all snapdragons it thrives in cool weather and declines once summer heat arrives, so plan bloom for spring or fall.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Potomac Snapdragon (Tall Single-Stem Greenhouse Cut-Flower Series)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before transplanting; surface sow without covering since seed needs light to germinate. Potomac performs as a single-stem crop under the cool temperatures of fall, winter, or early spring production and is often netted or strung for straight, unbranched stems.

directions: Potomac is a tall, vigorous F1 snapdragon series bred for commercial greenhouse and high-tunnel cut-flower production, producing long, thick, single unbranched stems topped with densely packed spurred florets in colors including Appleblossom, Ivory, Rose, White, Yellow, and Lavender. Growers typically use support netting and grow it as a single-stem crop; pinching is avoided so all of the plant's energy goes into one dominant spike reaching three to four feet. Its heavy stem strength and long vase life have made it a mainstay of florist-grade snapdragon production, distinct from shorter branching bedding types. Like other snapdragons it performs best in cool conditions and is typically scheduled for fall-through-spring harvest in mild climates or heated structures elsewhere.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: QIS Series Statice (Quartet Improved Compact Branching Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots, since statice resents root disturbance; transplant after hardening off into full sun and well-drained soil once frost danger has passed.

directions: QIS (Quartet Improved Statice) is a compact, uniform, well-branched F1 statice series bred specifically for commercial cut-flower and dried-flower production, sold as individual colors including QIS Yellow, QIS Rose, QIS Blue, QIS Purple, QIS White, QIS Apricot, and QIS Carmine Rose alongside a blended mix. Its shorter, more uniform habit than open-pollinated statice strains produces an unusually heavy yield of straight, evenly sized stems per plant, an advantage for growers harvesting for both fresh bouquets and everlasting dried arrangements. The papery calyces hold their saturated color for years once air-dried upside down in a warm, dark space. Highly salt- and drought-tolerant, it is a dependable choice for coastal cutting gardens and hot, dry summer sites alike.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Fortress Series Statice (Large-Flowered Robust Cut-Flower Statice)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost in cell trays or individual pots to avoid disturbing the taproot; transplant into full sun and well-drained soil after frost danger has passed.

directions: Fortress is a vigorous, large-flowered F1 statice series bred for professional cut-flower growers, producing taller, sturdier stems and noticeably bigger flower clusters than older open-pollinated statice strains. It is sold as separate colors, including Fortress Rose, Fortress Yellow, Fortress White, Fortress Deep Blue, and Fortress Lavender, each bred for uniform timing and heavy stem counts per plant across a single harvest window. The dense, papery calyx clusters hold both fresh and dried, retaining strong color for years when cut at full bloom and air-dried upside down out of direct light. Excellent heat, drought, and salt tolerance make it well suited to hot summer cutting gardens and seaside plantings alike.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers
